'''''Aucuba japonica''''', commonly called '''spotted laurel''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 8 January 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |location=Pocheon |pages=370 |access-date=26 January 2017 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]] |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |archivedate=25 May 2017 }}</ref> '''Japanese laurel''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''Japanese aucuba'''<ref name=GRIN/> or '''gold dust plant''' (U.S.), is a shrub ({{convert|1|–|5|m|ft|disp=comma|abbr=on}}) [[native plant|native]] to rich forest soils of moist valleys, thickets, by streams and near shaded moist rocks in [[China]], [[Korea]], and [[Japan]].<ref name=poisonivy>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=17884 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref> This is the [[species]] of ''[[Aucuba]]'' commonly seen in gardens - often in [[variegated]] form. The [[leaves]] are opposite, broad lanceolate, {{convert|5|–|8|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. ''Aucuba japonica'' are [[dioecious]]. The [[flower]]s are small, {{convert|4|–|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, each with four purplish-brown petals; they are produced in clusters of 10-30 in a loose [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]]. The [[fruit]] is a red [[drupe]] approximately {{convert|1|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter that is avoided by birds.<ref>{{cite book|last=Fell|first=Derek|title=The essential gardener|year=1992|publisher=Gramercy|isbn=0517693399}}</ref>

The golden [[variegation]] patterns are inherited from the mother plant. If the female plant is variegated, the seedlings will be variegated regardless of what the male looks like.  If the female plant is green and male is variegated, the seedlings will be green. This indicates that the cause of variegation is not under the control of the DNA of the [[Cell nucleus|nucleus]], but probably under the control of the [[chloroplast]]s where [[photosynthesis]] occurs. Chloroplasts float in the [[cytoplasm]] of each cell and are inherited from the female parent.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.uaex.uada.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/Aucuba-japonica-variegata-gold-dust-plant-01-15-2016.aspx |title=Plant of the Week: Aucuba japonica “Variegata,” Aucuba, Gold Dust Plant |website=uaex.uada.edu |access-date=2024-10-12}}</ref>

==History==
''Aucuba japonica'' was introduced into England in 1783 by [[Philip Miller]]'s pupil [[John Graeffer]], at first as a plant for a heated [[greenhouse]]. It became widely cultivated as the "gold plant" by 19th-century gardeners. The plants being grown were female, and it was a purpose of [[Robert Fortune]]'s botanizing trip to newly opened Japan in 1861 to locate a male. It was located in the garden of Dr. Hall, resident at Yokohama, and sent to the nursery of Standish & Noble at Bagshot, Surrey. The firm's mother plant was fertilized and displayed, covered with red berries, at Kensington in 1864, creating a sensation that climaxed in 1891 with the statement from the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s secretary, the Rev. W. Wilkes, "You can hardly have too much of it".<ref>Coats (1964) 1992.</ref> A reaction to its ubiquitous presence set in after World War II.{{Cn|date=March 2025}}

==Cultivation==
This plant is valued for its ability to thrive in the most difficult of garden environments, dry shade. It also copes with pollution and salt-laden coastal winds. It is often seen as an informal [[hedge]], but may also be grown indoors as a [[houseplant]].<ref>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> Today numerous [[cultivar]]s are available from garden centres. The most popular cultivar is 'Variegata', with yellow spots on the leaves;<ref>"...whose measled form is now so common that one hardly realizes that there is also an unspotted ''Aucuba'', which can be quite a handsome bush" (Coats 1992).</ref> this is a female clone, a similar male clone being named 'Maculata'. The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:

* 'Crotonifolia'<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/95525/Aucuba-japonica-Crotonifolia-(f-v)/Details|title=''Aucuba japonica'' 'Crotonifolia' (f/v) AGM}}</ref>
* 'Golden King'<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/82008/Aucuba-japonica-Golden-King-(m-v)/Details|title=''Aucuba japonica'' 'Golden King' (m/v) AGM}}</ref>
* 'Rozannie' – A self-fertile variety not requiring a pollinator, produces deep red berries against solid green, glossy foliage.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/63095/Aucuba-japonica-Rozannie-(f-m)/Details|title=''Aucuba japonica'' 'Rozannie' (f/m) AGM}}</ref> 

Other cultivars include:-
* [[Form (botany)|forma]] ''longifolia''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=2141|title=''Aucuba japonica'' f. ''longifolia''}}</ref>
* 'Mr. Goldstrike' – Male plant with leaves heavily speckled in yellow.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.monrovia.com/plant-catalog/plants/129/mr-goldstrike-aucuba/| title=Mr. Goldstrike Aucuba| publisher=Monrovia.com| access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref>
* 'Picturata' – Female plant with yellow foliage fringed with green.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.monrovia.com/plant-catalog/plants/130/picturata-aucuba/| title=Picturata Aucuba| publisher=Monrovia.com| access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref>
* 'Petite Jade' – Variety with narrower leaves than other species, slender, and serrated. Solid green, growing to 6 ft. tall (can reach 10 ft. after 20 or more years).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.monrovia.com/plant-catalog/plants/3648/petite-jade-aucuba/| title=Petite Jade Aucuba| publisher=Monrovia.com| access-date=2018-02-20}}</ref>
* 'February Star' – Female plant with narrow leaves and sparse dots of variegation.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/287934/Aucuba-japonica-February-Star-(f-v)/Details| title=February Star Aucuba| publisher=RHS.org.uk| access-date=2021-02-13}}</ref>

==Etymology==
''Japonica'' means 'from Japan'.<ref name= "gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  p 220</ref>
